title: Delivery Kit
path: Tools Used in Community Health Nursing

headings.title: Introduction to the Delivery Kit in Community Health
headings.content: In the context of community health nursing in Nigeria, maternal and neonatal mortality remain significant public health challenges, often exacerbated by home deliveries occurring in resource-limited settings. The clean delivery kit, frequently referred to as a "mama kit" or clean birth kit, is a low-cost, portable intervention designed to promote hygienic practices during childbirth outside of formal health facilities. Community health extension workers (CHEWs) and midwives play a pivotal role in distributing these kits and educating expectant mothers and traditional birth attendants (TBAs) on their importance. By providing essential sterile items in a single, compact package, the delivery kit bridges the gap between inaccessible health institutions and the reality of rural home births. Understanding the composition and proper utilization of the delivery kit is a fundamental competency for nursing students. It empowers healthcare providers to drastically reduce the incidence of puerperal sepsis, tetanus, and neonatal infections that claim the lives of mothers and infants daily. Furthermore, introduction to the delivery kit emphasizes the preventive model of community nursing, where simple tools combined with community health education yield profound improvements in survival rates. Nursing students must appreciate that these kits do not replace skilled attendance at birth, but rather serve as a vital harm-reduction strategy where access to a comprehensive emergency obstetric care facility is delayed or completely unavailable.

headings.title: Purposes and Objectives of Clean Delivery
headings.content: The fundamental purpose of clean delivery is anchored on the famous "clean chain" concept, which mirrors the surgical asepsis chain in hospital operating theatres. During childbirth, pathogens can easily be introduced into the reproductive tract and the newborn's umbilical stump via unwashed hands, unsterilized cutting instruments, dirty surfaces, or unclean applications to the cord. The primary objective is therefore to eliminate the "six cleans": clean hands, clean delivery surface, clean cord cutting instrument, clean cord tie, clean cloth to wrap the baby, and clean wiping material for the perineum. By strictly observing these principles, nursing professionals can drastically prevent devastating morbidities such as puerperal sepsis, neonatal tetanus, and omphalitis. In Nigerian rural communities where cultural practices might sometimes encourage the application of harmful substances like saliva, mud, or ash to the umbilical stump, clean delivery objectives also incorporate vital health education. The educational aspect ensures that caregivers understand why foreign contaminants must be kept away from the newborn. Ultimately, every objective of a clean delivery kit focuses on safeguarding the physiological transition of the neonate and protecting the postpartum mother from preventable infectious complications, aligning with global sustainable development goals for maternal and child health.

headings.title: Standard Components and Contents of a Delivery Kit
headings.content: A standard delivery kit contains carefully selected items designed to address the immediate needs of both mother and newborn during labor and delivery. While contents may vary slightly depending on regional health agency guidelines or specific non-governmental organization distributions, several components are universally mandatory. Typically, a kit includes a clean plastic sheet or mat to provide a barrier between the parturient woman and the floor, ensuring a clean surface. It also features a bar of soap for thorough handwashing by the birth attendant. For the management of the umbilical cord, the kit provides a sterile razor blade or scalpel for clean cutting, along with sterile threads or cord ties to secure the cord vessels safely. A clean piece of gauze or cotton wool is included for wiping the baby's eyes and face immediately after birth. In many Nigerian contexts, the kit may also contain a pair of examination gloves to protect the attendant and maintain barrier nursing principles, as well as a clean piece of cloth or baby wrapper to dry and wrap the newborn, preventing hypothermia. Nursing students must be able to inspect these components, verify their integrity, and recognize if any essential item is missing or compromised before the birth process begins.

headings.title: Aseptic Techniques and Infection Prevention
headings.content: Aseptic technique is the cornerstone of infection prevention when utilizing a delivery kit, especially in environments where running water and autoclaves are absent. Nursing students must understand that infection prevention is not merely about having sterile tools, but about the consistent execution of behaviors that prevent microbial contamination. Before touching the mother or opening the kit components, the birth attendant must perform rigorous hand hygiene using clean water and the soap provided in the kit, or an alcohol-based hand rub if available. Gloves, when present in the kit, must be worn correctly without contaminating their outer surfaces during donning. Throughout the delivery process, the "no-touch" technique should be applied whenever possible—meaning sterile items should only touch clean anatomical areas or other sterile surfaces. The delivery surface must be covered completely by the clean plastic sheet, and any equipment that drops onto the floor must be immediately discarded and never used. Particular attention must be given to the perineal area, which should be wiped gently from front to back to avoid introducing fecal pathogens into the birth canal. Practicing strict infection prevention protects the mother from postpartum endometritis and sepsis, while shielding the neonate from life-threatening systemic infections like tetanus and sepsis.

headings.title: Preparation and Inspection of the Kit Before Use
headings.content: Proper preparation and meticulous inspection of the delivery kit before use can mean the difference between a safe delivery and a catastrophic obstetric emergency. When labor begins, the community health nurse or birth attendant must first gather all necessary materials, including the delivery kit, clean water, extra cloths, and a safe receptacle for waste. The kit packaging must be carefully inspected for any signs of tears, punctures, moisture, or damage that could compromise the sterility of its internal contents. Expiry dates on sterilized items or components like gloves must be verified; expired components must be discarded and replaced immediately. The birth environment must be prepared by ensuring adequate lighting, privacy, and a clean, draft-free space where the plastic sheet from the kit can be securely spread. The attendant must set up the sterile items in an organized, logical sequence so they can be accessed smoothly without frantic searching during the critical moments of childbirth. Preparing the mother psychologically by explaining each step and reassuring her is equally important to reduce anxiety and promote cooperation. By conducting this thorough pre-use inspection, the nurse ensures that all tools function correctly, sterility is guaranteed, and potential complications are anticipated before they manifest.

headings.title: Step-by-Step Utilization During Childbirth
headings.content: Utilizing the delivery kit step-by-step during childbirth requires calm, focused, and systematic execution by the healthcare provider. As labor progresses to the second stage and crowning occurs, the birth attendant must ensure hands are thoroughly washed and gloves are worn. The clean plastic sheet from the kit is spread beneath the mother's buttocks to protect the field. As the baby's head emerges, the attendant supports the perineum and allows natural restitution and expulsion without performing aggressive, routine maneuvers that could cause lacerations. Once the baby is fully delivered, the infant is placed immediately on the mother's abdomen or chest skin-to-skin, provided there are no complications. The baby's mouth and nose may be gently wiped using a clean gauze piece from the kit if secretions obstruct breathing. Delaying cord clamping for one to three minutes (or until cord pulsation stops) allows for optimal placental transfusion, which boosts the newborn's iron stores. Using the sterile blade and cord ties from the kit, the umbilical cord is securely tied at two points—one about 2 cm and the other about 5 cm from the baby's abdomen—and cut cleanly between the ties. Continuous observation of both mother and newborn is maintained as they await the third stage of labor and placental delivery.

headings.title: Immediate Postpartum Care and Newborn Management
headings.content: Immediate postpartum care and newborn management are critical phases where timely interventions save lives. Following the delivery of the placenta, the nurse must assess the uterus to ensure it is firmly contracted, thereby preventing postpartum hemorrhage (PPH), which is a leading cause of maternal mortality in Nigeria. The mother's vital signs, vaginal bleeding, and general condition must be monitored closely every 15 minutes for the first hour. For the newborn, immediate management focuses on maintaining warmth, establishing breathing, and initiating early breastfeeding. The baby should be dried thoroughly using a clean cloth from the delivery kit to prevent hypothermia through evaporation. Skin-to-skin contact should be maintained, as it regulates the baby's temperature, stabilizes heart rate, and promotes bonding. The newborn's eyes should be wiped clean, and prophylactic eye care administered if available. Early initiation of breastfeeding within the first hour of life should be encouraged and assisted, ensuring the infant receives colostrum, which is rich in protective antibodies. The umbilical stump must be inspected for any active bleeding and kept clean and dry, strictly avoiding the application of unhygienic substances like saliva, herbs, or toothpaste. Nursing students must document all findings accurately and educate the family on danger signs that require immediate referral to a higher health facility.

headings.title: Maintenance, Replenishment, and Disposal Guidelines
headings.content: Proper maintenance, timely replenishment, and safe disposal guidelines conclude the lifecycle of a delivery kit and protect the community from biohazard risks. Once childbirth is completed, all single-use items such as plastic sheets, gauzes, and packaging materials must be handled as infectious medical waste and disposed of according to local healthcare waste management protocols. Used razor blades or cutting instruments must be placed immediately into a puncture-resistant safety box (sharps container) to prevent accidental needle-stick or sharp injuries to healthcare workers, family members, or waste scavengers. Reusable items, if any are included in specific kits, must undergo thorough decontamination, cleaning, and high-level disinfection or sterilization before being stored again. For community health programs and clinics, maintaining adequate stock levels requires regular inventory checks to ensure kits are reordered and restocked well before expiry dates are reached. Storage areas for unissued kits must be cool, dry, and clean, protecting the sterile barriers from moisture, direct sunlight, and rodent damage. Nursing students must understand that improper disposal of delivery waste can spread blood-borne pathogens like HIV and Hepatitis B, making safe waste management an essential public health responsibility.
